document.title: Post-Technical Conference Comments and Responses to Commission Questions of LS Power Development, LLC re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
POST-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE COMMENTS AND RESPONSES TO 
COMMISSION QUESTIONS OF LS POWER DEVELOPMENT, LLC (“LS 
POWER”) 
LS Power appreciates the opportunity to participate in the continuing dialogue around PJM 
governance.1  While we have provided in-depth responses to specific questions posed by the 
Commission, below we provide context for those responses: 
1. Independence: The good news: every participant in the PJM market, from government, to 
stakeholders to management to Board believes it is imperative that the PJM Board be independent.  
But that begs the question: independent of whom?  LS Power believes that the PJM Board has an 
obligation to try to understand the various goals and objectives of policy makers, stakeholders and 
PJM management (“Interested PJM Parties”), but the Board is obligated to make the best decision 
for PJM’s core mission of creating and operating robust, competitive and non-discriminatory electric 
power markets, while understanding customer needs and delivering valued service in a cost efficient-
manner.2  While decisions must consider all of the positions of the Interested PJM Parties, the Board 
itself must not be influenced – or concerned about responses -- by any one of the Interested PJM 
Parties.  For this reason, LS Power does not support open meetings or the publication of Board votes, 
as described in more detail below. 
LS Power reiterates its previously submitted comments that creating a Market Surveillance 
Committee to directly advise the Board would provide more of such independence: such a committee 
would not be beholden to stakeholders, policy makers, the Independent Market Monitor or PJM 
management in helping the Board understand and make decisions around very technical issues.  LS 
Power welcomes the opportunity to work with the Commission and stakeholders to create such a 
committee.   
2. Communications.  Again, there is almost unanimous agreement on another issue: communications in 
the PJM process must be enhanced.  The PJM Board and OPSI need to find a more satisfactory path 
to effective communications.  Moreover, ex-parte rules between the PJM Board and stakeholders 
should be relaxed.  As noted in our Initial Comments,3 other Regional Transmission Operators 
provide examples of greater interaction among stakeholders and Board members without 
 
1 All terms used herein shall have the meaning set forth in the PJM Operating Agreement. PJM, Amended and 
Restated Operating Agreement, Rate Schedule FERC No. 24, (eff. 7/14/2011) (“Operating Agreement”). 
2 See, https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm  
3 Pre-Technical Conference Comments of Marjorie Philips, LS Power Development, LLC, at 6, Docket No. AD26-7-
000 (F.E.R.C. filed July 14, 2026).

compromising Board Integrity.  LS Power would rather the Commission allow stakeholders to 
develop better ex-parte rules rather than have this be a topic of Settlement discussions. 
 
3. State Participation in the PJM Process.  As stated in our Comments and by many participants at the 
Technical Conference,4 the states can and should play a critical role in PJM.  LS Power urges the 
Commission to facilitate the creation of a better funded and technically enhanced OPSI so that the 
states have more meaningful representation on technical market matters.  PJM and OPSI should 
develop a more structured and effective process for discussing PJM matters.   While understanding 
that some participants believe the states need an additional voice to their state commissions 
participating in OPSI, LS Power does not support such an approach.  For one, states should speak 
with a unified voice.  None of the Interested PJM Parties want to pursue a path and then find out that 
a state was not confident in a proposal.  LS Power believes that the OPSI rules should be amended to 
allow for state participation beyond state commissioners, and it is up to OPSI and the state 
representatives to develop an efficient approach.  While the states do not meet the requirements 
under the Federal Power Act to be granted the ability to file 205 rights5, LS Power is on the record 
for allowing states more direct involvement in cost allocation of transmission projects and a formal 
advisory role on other matters.  Nonetheless, the change in composition does not mean the Board 
must endorse OPSI positions, but it must take them into consideration.  States always have the right 
to file comments in 205 proceedings, or to initiate a 206 proceeding. 
 
4. The PJM Nominating Committee.  LS Power is concerned that the state representatives want a vote 
on the Nominating Committee for misplaced reasons.  It appears they would like to drive state-
specific policy by having a say on who becomes a Board member.  The PJM Code of Conduct for 
the Nominating Committee could not be more explicit:  The members of the Nominating Committee 
shall undertake and fulfill their duties in furtherance of the best interests of PJM without regard to 
the individual or affiliated company interests of any member of the Nominating Committee and 
without regard to the interests of any other PJM member or group of PJM members.6 LS Power 
supports the current approach to board member selection.  It is important that candidates meet 
specific experience and technical requirements for filling a particular Board seat when it becomes 
open.   Another important factor is independence – if a candidate has taken consistent specific 
positions over the years, they should be evaluated on the basis of whether those positions might bias 
a decision as a Board member.  Finally, as employees of LS Power have participated in the 
Nominating Committee and can attest: the five sector representatives of the Nominating Committee 
focus on how the nominee’s integrity, leadership, and personality would fit with the Board.  And 
while it is true that industrial customers can represent the End Use Sector, Consumer Advocates can, 
and have served on the Nominating Committee, directly representing consumer interests.  A further 
discussion is provided in our response below. 
 
5. 205 Rights.  LS Power believes that the current allocation of 205 rights in PJM achieves the right 
balance, although we would support – short of explicit 205 rights – more direct involvement of the 
 
4 Commission-Led Technical Conference on PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Panel 1, Docket No. AD26-7-
000, at (Fed. Energy Regul. Comm'n July 23, 2026) (“Technical Conference”). 
5 Federal Power Act § 201(a), 16 U.S.C. § 824(a). 
6 https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/nc/postings/charter.pdf.

states in terms of transmission cost allocation.  PJM is a regional organization, however, and 
ultimately all Interested PJM Parties benefit from this structure.  Thus, state involvement in rate 
structure must respect the principles behind any cost allocation approach and not simply seek to 
avoid costs.   Nonetheless, there is an impression that the Board needs to obtain 205 rights over the 
Operating Agreement to expedite decision making.  In our response, we address this and have 
diligently researched best practices and Commission precedents from other markets. From our 
research, we believe that the governance framework that the CAISO Board Policy approved on 
December 18, 2015, with authorization from FERC, in its Charter for WEIM and EDAM 
Governance (Section 2.2.2(i)) provides strong precedent for providing Section 205 filing rights  to a 
unanimous PJM Board in the case of stakeholder impasse and “exigent circumstances exist such that 
a tariff amendment is critical to preserve reliability or to protect market integrity.”7  In our comments 
below, we provide this research and translate the WEIM and EDAM governance concept into PJM 
Operating Agreement language that could be applied to a PJM context with the PJM Members 
Committee.  In any case, we note that PJM always has Section 206 rights, they have exercised them 
and can do so at any time.8 
 
PJM has filed with FERC, in recent years, attempts to move the exclusive rights of the Members 
Committee related to regional transmission planning to PJM.  FERC rejected these attempts, and the 
DC Circuit has also upheld the Members Committee.  Given the consumer impact of transmission 
and the importance of robust alternatives discussion, LS Power believes that the regional 
transmission planning filing rights are appropriately now with the Members Committee.   However, 
consistent with our 2024 filed comments in EL24-119-00 and ER24-23389, we believe that the 
Members Committee could grant the unanimous PJM Board the right to make a limited Section 205 
Operating Agreement filing to preserve reliability or protect market integrity in the case of exigent 
circumstances, a stakeholder impasse, and unanimous PJM Board support (akin to the Western EIM 
structure discussed in greater detail below). 
As noted in our response below, LS Power provides specific language to address potential 205 rights 
of the Board in similar circumstances.  Likewise, for the reasons noted in our response below, OPSI 
should not be granted 205 rights. 
 
 
7 Charter for WEIM and EDAM Governance § 2.2.2(i) (Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., Policy Adopted Dec. 18, 2015, 
as amended). The weblink can be found at: https://www.westernenergymarkets.com/documents/charter-for-
weim-and-edam-governance.pdf 
8 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Section 206 Filing Alleging that the Locational Deliverability Area Reliability 
Requirement Is Unjust and Unreasonable as Applied in a Particular Locational Deliverability Area in the 2024/2025 
Base Residual Auction, and Requesting that the Commission Establish a Refund Effective Date, Docket No. 
EL23-19-000 (filed Dec. 23, 2022). 
9 Protest of LS Power Development, LLC, Rolling Hills Generating, LLC, and Central Transmission as filed July 22, 
2024, EL24-119-000 and ER24-2338-000, page 27. 
https://elibrary.ferc.gov/eLibrary/filelist?accession_number=20240722-5201&optimized=false&sid=8f4156dc-b47e-
4b26-ba12-a76791e5af5c

6. Board Term.  PJM has offered terms for settlement discussion, which includes a tenure of nine (9) 
years for Board Members.  LS Power strongly opposes such a lengthy term, which is even longer 
than the term of a FERC Commissioner.  Such a term length could diminish the pool of candidates 
who are willing to commit to serving for so long on the Board.   Moreover, no other Regional 
Transmission Operator has such long terms for their Board.10 The strong rationale for a shorter 
tenure extends beyond the world of RTOs.  For example, the Securities and Exchange Commission 
(the “SEC”), in opining on the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, expresses a concern about the 
relationship between auditor and client, noting:  "We believe that a proper balance is one that weighs 
the responsibility for decisions on accounting and financial reporting issues impacting the financial 
statements with the level of the relationship with senior management of the client."11  This is 
analogous to the concern stakeholders have about a Board member’s relationship with PJM 
management potentially coloring their judgment.  In that regard, Congress believed that a five-year 
term of audit was better than seven years, mandating the five-year rotation, and the SEC in 
implementing it established the matching five-year cooling off period.  Similarly, the United 
Kingdom Corporate Code of Governance recommends annual re-election for Board members and a 
limit of nine years for the Chairperson.12   Finally, a term of such a duration would create an 
immunity from the performance review that exists in very little parts of our world: corporate 
directors are voted on, management is fired for non-performance, governmental officials are not re-
elected, and even governmental agency commissioners may be removed without cause by the 
President.13 
 
 
 
10  
LS Power notes that NYISO currently has the longest Board term length of four years, which with 
renomination limits total tenure of a board member in that ISO to 12-years.  All of the other RTOs have a maximum 
tenure of nine years with term lengths set at three years.  See, Governance Structure and Practices in the FERC 
Jurisdictional ISOs/RTOs February 2021, Prepared for NESCOE by: Christopher A. Parent Katherine S. Fisher, 
William R. Cotton, Cali C. Clar, Exeter Associates, Inc. (February 2021),Page ES 5.  
11 Securities and Exchange Commission, Strengthening the Commission's Requirements Regarding Auditor 
Independence, Release Nos. 33-8183; 34-47265; 35-27642; IC-25915; IA-2103; File No. S7-49-02, 68 Fed. Reg. 
6006, 6019 (Feb. 5, 2003). 
12 UK Corporate Governance Code, January 2024, The Financial Reporting Council Limited 2024, Provision 18 
13  Emily P. Mallen, Stephen Hug & Corban Coffman, Slaughtering the Independent Agency? What Trump v. Slaughter 
Means for FERC, Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld LLP (July 7, 2026), 
https://www.akingump.com/en/insights/blogs/speaking-energy/slaughtering-the-independent-agency-what-trump-v-
slaughter-means-for-ferc.

II. RESPONSES TO SPECIFIC QUESTIONS IN APPENDIX 
# 
Question / Theme 
LS Power Position 
1 
Should Board members' terms be 
extended to five or more years? 
Yes 
 
Comment: 
LS Power supports a 5 year term.  Many new Board members are not familiar with the PJM markets.  They must invest 
significant time learning them and require time to gain the knowledge of PJM’s operations to make quality decisions.  
Stakeholders benefit from having Board members with institutional knowledge, which a three year tenure is less likely to 
provide.   A term longer than five years is less preferable because it may make Board members less accountable for their 
decisions because of security in a long term and increasing reliance on PJM management.  PJM Board members are well paid, 
and we would not want to see a long term provide incentives to be less proactive over the duration of the term. The risk to 
extending the 3 year term is precisely that: Board members can “coast” on a longer term.  LS Power’s support is based on the 
expectation that the Board will be diligent and “self-police” members that are not contributing according to the requirements of 
the role. 
2 
Should there be a maximum number 
of years that a Board member may 
serve (e.g., 10 years)? 
Yes 
 
Comment: 
As a preliminary matter, LS Power supports the option to retain board members at the end of the 5 year term, indicating 
confidence from stakeholders.  Generally, however, with a five year term, Board members should only serve two terms. 
Extension of the initial term will allow for renomination where the board member demonstrates impressive engagement and 
institutional knowledge, while the overall term limit ensures that fresh perspectives are continually introduced to the Board. 
3 
Should Board member qualification 
rules be revised to provide a 
preference for some Board members 
that reside in the PJM region? 
Yes 
 
Comment: 
LS Power supports the expression of a preference, not a mandate.  We would note that one current Board member resides in 
Chicago. 
4 
Should conflict-of-interest rules be 
revised to reduce the cooling off 
period for Board members from two 
years to one year? 
Yes, with a qualification 
 
Comment: 
LS Power is concerned about the potential of a Board Member looking for employment with a Member company while still 
sitting on the Board.  This is an obvious conflict of interest.  LS Power could support a one year cooling off period provided that 
solicitation for employment by the Board member or the Member Company does not occur until after the Board member’s term 
has terminated. 
5 
Should restrictions on Board 
communications be relaxed to enable 
Yes

more communication between the 
Board and stakeholders? 
 
Comment: 
PJM’s culture and ex-parte rules were founded on the belief that Board members would be unable to make independent 
judgments if they engaged with stakeholders outside of the stakeholder process.  LS Power believes that the culture and process 
of other RTOs that enable greater Board and stakeholder interaction demonstrates otherwise.  Please see our Technical 
Conference comments on suggestions for improving interactions. 
6 
In order to increase transparency, 
should Board votes be made public or 
the Board be required to explain its 
reasoning? 
No/Yes 
 
Comment: 
The Board votes should not be made public.  This could undermine the independent decision making of individual Board 
members, especially if they are allowed to seek another term.  Moreover, if Board interaction with stakeholders is relaxed, 
revealing a Board member’s decisions could lead to greater lobbying.  Instead, the Board should be required to explain its 
reasoning. LS Power would like to understand what the Board considered, whether it was a unanimous decision immediately, 
and if not, what the discussion focused on and the factors that led to the final decision.   
7 
In order to increase transparency, 
should some Board meetings be open 
or available to the public? 
No 
 
Comment: 
LS Power believes that for the Board to remain independent, substantive policy-making meetings should not be open.  
Stakeholders have some insight into Board thinking through the Liaison Committee meetings already as do the states through 
direct meetings between OPSI and the Board, but an open format likely will result in performative meetings and will eliminate 
the ability of the Board to meaningfully discuss and debate issues. 
8 
Should PJM's governing documents be 
revised to explicitly state that the 
responsibility of PJM and its Board is 
to serve the public interest? 
No 
 
Comment: 
LS Power is concerned that “public interest” means different things to different Interested PJM Parties.  For example, the 
Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative could be in the “public interest” in some states, but not in others.  And in some states, it is 
not even a permanent policy.  Rather, PJM management and the Board must be accountable to adhere to PJM’s mission as an 
RTO under the Federal Power Act, which is to produce the lowest reasonable wholesale rates for the benefit of consumers in the 
region for which it is responsible. We would note that at the August 19 Members Committee meeting, the Members strongly 
endorsed language that explicitly declares the Board’s duties and responsibilities to include “the creation and operation of a 
robust, competitive, and non-discriminatory electric power market that is designed and operated for the benefit of 
consumers in the PJM region”14 in accordance with the Federal Power Act. 
 
14 August 19, 2026 PJM Members Committee meeting, Item 1, Emphasis added (Available at 
https://www.pjm.com/forms/registration/Meeting%20Registration.aspx?ID={75530C8F-4A89-4475-959B-CF80D731EA4F} with 
voting results shown at https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mc/2026/20260819/20260819-mc-
voting-results--agenda-item-1b.pdf )

9 
Should state representatives have at 
least one voting member on the 
Nominating Committee? 
No, with a qualification 
  
Comment: 
LS Power would support unequivocally an OPSI nominated representative to observe discussions at the Nominating 
Committee.  Because of concerns with the Freedom of Information Act,15 this person would not be allowed to receive written 
materials or take notes in order to protect the confidential identification of candidates and the content of Nominating Committee 
deliberations.   
LS Power also could support OPSI appointing someone not currently employed by the state or federal government to be a 
voting member, provided that person adhered to the confidentiality requirements of serving on the Nominating Committee and 
the proper safeguards were put in place to ensure that confidentiality would be maintained despite their association with the 
governmental representatives. 
If a settlement agreement provides that a sitting governmental member may participate and vote on the Nominating Committee, 
LS Power advocates that that person be the Chairperson of OPSI and that additional confidentiality requirements are 
implemented to protect against FOIA requests for the reasons stated above. 
10 
Should PJM adopt public performance 
metrics and tie management 
compensation to their achievement? 
Yes/No 
 
Comment: 
Publishing performance metrics would clarify PJM priorities.  However, the Board should exercise its exclusive discretion over 
PJM management compensation.   
11 
Should the stakeholder process be 
advisory, i.e., stakeholder votes only 
inform the Board? 
No, with a qualification 
 
Comment: 
Currently, the PJM Members Committee has exclusive 205 rights over the Operating Agreement.  This includes all energy 
product market rules, and transmission planning.  It excludes all operational and reliability rules, over which the Board retains 
205 rights.  The stakeholder process provides a good check and balance approach to these markets.  However, LS Power shares 
the frustration that sometimes enhancements and even necessary modifications can be trapped in a long stakeholder process.  
We would support discussion around a process that determines when the stakeholders are at an impasse and a unanimous PJM 
Board should have the 205 rights and is further discussed under Question 13, below.  In any case, PJM still retains 206 rights.   
12 
Should PJM have section 205 filing 
rights over energy and ancillary 
services unencumbered by the 2/3 
Members Committee approval? 
No, please see Question 11, above and Question 13 below 
13 
Should PJM have section 205 filing 
rights over Regional Transmission 
Expansion Planning (RTEP) 
unencumbered by 2/3 Members 
Committee approval? 
No 
 
 
15 Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. § 552 (2018).

Comment: 
As noted above, LS Power would support language similar to what exists in the Western EIM structure, modified to apply to 
PJM: 
  
LS Power Proposed OA language (akin to the Western EIM structure16): 
The PJM Board alone may authorize a FERC filing if, and only if, all of the following conditions are met: (i) The PJM Board, 
by unanimous vote, promptly notifies the Members Committee and makes a finding that the Members Committee has reached 
an impasse and that exigent circumstances exist such that a unanimous PJM Board Section 205 tariff or OA amendment is 
critical to preserve reliability or to protect market integrity. Unless the circumstance is so time critical as to require immediate 
action, this finding may be made only after PJM Board management has presented an initiative to the Members Committee a 
second time in an effort to propose a tariff or OA change on an issue that the Members Committee has authority to approve. In 
such a time-critical circumstance where there is not sufficient time to develop and vote on a revised proposal, the Board may by 
unanimous vote approve a PJM Board Section 205 tariff or OA amendment filing on an expedited basis without completing the 
second attempt to find an acceptable proposal. (ii) The Board must set forth the basis for any and all of its findings justifying 
exigent or time critical circumstances in writing and PJM shall be under no Common Interest Agreement with any PJM 
Member. (iii) If the Board authorizes such a filing, the FERC filing shall include any written opinion or other statement the PJM 
Members Committee may decide to offer regarding the proposed tariff amendment. The PJM Members Committee shall have 
the option to retain outside counsel to assist in preparing any written opinion or statement on the proposed tariff amendment that 
it decides to include in the filing. 
14 
Should OPSI have 'jump ball' rights 
over resource adequacy and 
transmission cost allocation filings 
when a supermajority of OPSI agrees? 
No 
 
Comment: 
OPSI does not sell any products in the wholesale market, so it would be inappropriate to provide OPSI 205 rights, formally or 
informally.  It is important to remember that policies are different among the states, and in fact can change within a state after 
an election.  Designing a market around changing policy goals can only undermine market fundamentals.  LS Power supports a 
broadened role for the states in determining transmission cost allocation.  Cost allocation, contrary to resource adequacy, is 
about a current allocation at the time it is accrued – not about effectuating long term rule changes.  As noted earlier, LS Power 
also supports providing OPSI with greater direct input to the PJM Board, as articulated in our comments. 
15 
Should the Members Committee have 
'jump ball' filing rights over portions 
of the tariff where PJM has 205 rights 
when a supermajority approves an 
alternative? 
Yes 
 
Comment: 
LS Power believes that regardless of whether the Members Committee should receive jump ball rights, it should have outside 
counsel advising it, similar to NEPOOL in New England.  Availability of counsel makes even more sense if PJM Board is given 
any type of 205 rights over the Operating Agreement in the case of stakeholder impasse and exigent circumstances existing such 
that a tariff amendment is critical to preserve reliability or to protect market integrity.  
16 
Should the approval threshold in the 
Members Committee be lowered from 
two-thirds sector-weighted voting? 
No 
 
16 Charter for WEIM and EDAM Governance § 2.2.2(i) (Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., Policy Adopted Dec. 18, 2015, as 
amended). The weblink can be found at: https://www.westernenergymarkets.com/documents/charter-for-weim-and-edam-
governance.pdf

Comment: 
The current super-majority voting requirement drives the stakeholder process to consensus on the critical issues that make it as 
far as the Members Committee.  Lowering that voting threshold would dilute the incentive for collaboration and undermine 
PJM’s ability to facilitate discussions that resolve the greatest number of issues that emerge in the stakeholder process. 
17 
Should the voting rules barring 
affiliate votes, which apply to senior 
standing committees, also apply to 
lower-level committees? 
Yes 
Comment: 
Removing the affiliate voting rules at the lower-level committees will necessitate the involvement of significantly more 
stakeholder participants in each of those lower-level committees, who do not currently actively engage in those conversations.  
That engagement will enhance issue identification and the prioritizing of issues for development and increase the likelihood that 
once those issues reach the higher-level committees, that they will be successfully acted upon. 
18 
In addition to OPSI, should there be a 
second state representative group 
consisting of governors' 
representatives and/or state 
legislators? 
No 
 
Comment: 
As was discussed by PJM President David Mills, Commissioner Judy Chang, and LS Power at the Technical Conference, there 
should not be two different voices speaking for the states.  Instead, OPSI’s by-laws and rules should be amended to allow for 
the meaningful participation of the state representatives that the states would like to represent them in the PJM stakeholder 
discussions. 
19 
Should state representatives have a 
formal voting role in the stakeholder 
process (limited to certain topics) in 
addition to consumer advocate votes? 
No 
 
Comment: 
LS Power supports greater funding for the OPSI organization so its members can have more meaningful participation in 
stakeholder discussions.  OPSI should have meaningful representation in lower committees.  Nothing undercuts stakeholders’ 
ability to arrive at a decision more than a vote or proposal that is outside the normal course of stakeholder deliberations. 
20 
Should PJM be required to consult 
with OPSI prior to making a Section 
205 filing related to resource adequacy 
and transmission cost allocation? 
Yes 
 
Comment: 
LS Power supports a formal consultation pathway between OPSI and the Board.  As was noted at the Technical Conference by 
PJM President Mills and OPSI Chairwoman Bagot, communications have not been effective.  Both OPSI and the Board need to 
commit to developing better ways of communicating.  That said, the Board should take into account OPSI’s positions and 
advocacy but ultimately must exercise its independent decision making.

III. CONCLUSION 
LS Power believes that enhancements to PJM governance are necessary, including explicit rules for state 
engagement with stakeholders and the Board, as well as for decision making in the stakeholder process itself.  
That said, governance enhancements should not be a distraction from the more critical issues facing PJM: 
ensuring its competitive markets will ensure reliability and result in the lowest reasonable cost for 
consumers.  LS Power reiterates our comments previously filed with FERC: PJM is responsible for 
wholesale rates.  PJM’s and the PJM Board’s mandate is to ensure that the markets it administers are 
efficient and produce the least reasonable cost.  It is the states’ responsibility to design retail rates that meet 
their affordability policy goals.  To advance the conversation on effective governance, we have introduced 
specific Operating Agreement language that would trigger in the event of Board unanimity in the face of 
impending reliability or market harm.  As such, we respectfully ask for consideration of our proposed OA 
language discussed herein. 
Respectfully submitted,  
/s/  Marjorie R. Philips
